name: Kochi
tagline: Spice-trade port where colonial Kerala meets the sea.
whenBlurb: October to March is dry and pleasant, with the Biennale and Cochin Carnival crowning winter; avoid the heavy June-September monsoon downpours.

ourTake.lede: Kochi is the most walkable and cosmopolitan corner of Kerala, and Fort Kochi deserves a slow two days on foot rather than a rushed stopover before the backwaters. Time your first evening for the Chinese fishing nets at sunset, but spend the days in the spice-trade lanes, the churches and synagogue, and the excellent contemporary art spaces. It is a good soft landing before or after the houseboats.
ourTake.comeIf: You want Kerala's history and harbour life as a gentle gateway to the backwaters.
ourTake.skipIf: You want nightlife or a beach holiday; this is a quiet, cultural port town.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Brunton Boatyard
credentials: CGH Earth heritage hotel, leased from the Port Trust 1992, opened 1999
26 rooms, all harbour-facing, on the site of the original Brunton boatyard
History restaurant, dishes from the 32 communities of Fort Kochi
items.description: CGH Earth's heritage flagship on a 19th-century colonial boatyard, every one of its 26 rooms faces the harbour and the Chinese fishing nets.

items.name: The Malabar House
credentials: Relais & Châteaux, the first Indian member (accepted 1997)
Fort Kochi's original boutique heritage hotel
Home to The Malabar Junction, its Relais & Châteaux restaurant
items.description: The first Indian hotel accepted into Relais & Châteaux, an 18th-century mansion turned art-filled boutique of just 17 rooms.

items.name: Taj Malabar Resort & Spa, Cochin
credentials: Taj Hotels / IHCL, heritage wing built 1935, reopened after a year-long 2024 renovation
93 rooms and suites with waterfront views
Rice Boat, celebrated Kerala coastal-seafood restaurant
items.description: Cochin's grand harbour hotel since 1935, a 2024-renovated Taj wrapping Ernakulam's waterfront, with an infinity pool over the backwaters.

items.name: Grand Hyatt Kochi Bolgatty
credentials: Hyatt, Grand Hyatt, 264 rooms including suites and four plunge-pool villas
Overlooking Vembanad Lake on 26 acres
Santata Spa, 1,000+ sq m, Ayurvedic and Western therapies
items.description: The city's largest luxury resort, 264 rooms on 26 waterfront acres of Bolgatty Island, with villas that have private plunge pools.

items.name: Old Harbour Hotel
credentials: Heritage mansion, ~300 years old, the first hotel of old Cochin
13 rooms, each named for a Fort Kochi street
Restaurant 1788, seafood-led, with classical music at dinner
items.description: A 300-year-old Dutch-Portuguese mansion, Fort Kochi's first hotel, 13 characterful rooms around a garden and pool.

items.name: Xandari Harbour
credentials: Housed in two ~century-old wharf spice warehouses
16 rooms with harbour or garden views
Restaurant 51, farm-to-table Malabar cuisine with a riverside balcony
items.description: Two century-old spice warehouses reborn as a 16-room boutique, an infinity pool and courtyard opening straight onto the water.

items.name: Forte Kochi
credentials: Paul John Resorts & Hotels, heritage boutique on Princess Street
Portuguese-Dutch-British mansion, once a Jewish family home
27 rooms; walking distance to the fishing nets and Mahatma Gandhi Beach
items.description: A Portuguese-era mansion on Princess Street, restored by Paul John into a 27-room heritage boutique in the heart of the fort.

items.name: Kayal Island Retreat
credentials: National Geographic, 'Around the World in 24 Hours' (the only Indian entry), for the Kakkathuruthu sunset
Condé Nast Traveller recognition, lakeside boutique
Four cottages on a private backwater island; reached by traditional rowboat
items.description: A four-cottage island hideaway on Vembanad Lake, reached only by rowboat, the sunset Nat Geo named one of the world's best.

items.name: The Chinese Fishing Nets (Cheena Vala)
items.description: The cantilevered shore-operated nets along the Fort Kochi waterfront are the city's signature image, teak-and-bamboo frames worked by teams of fishermen, thought to have arrived with traders from Kublai Khan's court centuries ago. Come at dusk when the light drops behind the harbour mouth and the silhouettes are at their most cinematic; the freshest catch is grilled to order at the stalls right beside them.

items.name: St Francis Church
credentials: India's oldest European-built church (early 16th century)
items.description: The oldest European-built church in India, put up by Portuguese friars in the early 1500s, and the spot where Vasco da Gama was first buried before his remains were taken to Lisbon, his gravestone is still set in the floor. A cool, spare, whitewashed interior with old punkah cloth-fans overhead; a quiet ten minutes of deep history off Fort Kochi's main green.

items.name: Santa Cruz Cathedral Basilica
items.description: One of only a handful of basilicas in Kerala, twin white spires outside, and inside a ceiling of pastel frescoes and Gothic arches that feel more Iberian than Indian. It stands beside St Francis Church, so the two make a natural pairing on a slow morning walk through the old quarter.

items.name: A Fort Kochi Heritage Walk
items.description: The whole peninsula is really an open-air museum of Portuguese, Dutch and British layers, bungalows with wooden verandahs, godowns, cemeteries and coir-scented lanes. A guided morning walk (or an unhurried self-led wander from Vasco da Gama Square down the parade ground) is the best way to read the town; heritage stays like Malabar House and Brunton Boatyard sit right in the thick of it.

items.name: Vasco da Gama Square & the parade ground
items.description: The narrow seafront promenade beside the fishing nets, lined with fresh-catch stalls, tender-coconut carts and ice-cream sellers, opening onto the old colonial parade ground. It is where Fort Kochi comes out to watch the sunset, an easy, atmospheric stroll before dinner at one of the heritage-hotel terraces.

items.name: Princess Street & Loafer's Corner
items.description: One of the oldest streets in Fort Kochi, a run of bronze-plastered European houses now given over to curio shops, cafes and small galleries, meeting at Loafer's Corner where Princess, Peter Celli and Bastion Streets converge under a balconied heritage building. The most walkable, photogenic stretch for browsing and a slow coffee.

items.name: Indo-Portuguese Museum
items.description: Set in the grounds of the Bishop's House, this small, well-kept museum gathers altarpieces, vestments, carved wood and silver from Kerala's Latin Catholic churches, the clearest single account of the Portuguese imprint on the coast. Quiet, air-conditioned and rarely crowded, an easy hour between the churches.

items.name: The Mattancherry (Dutch) Palace & its murals
items.description: Built for the Kochi rajas in the mid-1500s and reworked by the Dutch, its plain exterior hides some of the finest temple murals in India, dense, glowing panels of the Ramayana and Mahabharata covering the royal chambers. Photography is barred inside, which only sharpens the attention; the coronation hall and palanquins evoke the old spice-port court.

items.name: The Paradesi Synagogue
items.description: India's oldest active synagogue, from 1568, its floor laid with hand-painted blue-and-white Chinese tiles no two of which are alike, hung with Belgian glass lamps and fronted by a Dutch clock tower whose four faces carry Hebrew, Roman, Malayalam and Arabic numerals. A moving relic of Kochi's near-vanished Malabari and Paradesi Jewish community. Closed Fridays, Saturdays and Jewish holidays.

items.name: Jew Town & the antiques quarter
items.description: The lanes leading to the synagogue are a treasure hunt of dealers, rosewood cabinets, brass and bronze, old maps, temple lamps, nautical instruments and colonial curios, alongside spice-scented cafes. Serious collectors ship home genuine restored pieces; browsers get one of the most characterful shopping walks in India.

items.name: The Mattancherry spice markets
items.description: The godowns and open shopfronts behind Jew Town still trade Kerala's pepper, cardamom, cloves, ginger and turmeric, the very commerce that drew the Portuguese and Dutch here five centuries ago. The air is thick with it; buy graded whole spices at source, far better than anything back home.

items.name: A Kathakali performance
items.description: Kerala's dance-drama of green-and-crimson painted faces, elaborate costume and a whole language of eye and hand gestures. The best centres let you arrive early to watch the hour-long make-up ritual, then narrate the story before the show so it never feels opaque, a genuinely spellbinding evening, and children are often riveted.

items.name: A Kalaripayattu demonstration
items.description: Kerala's ancient martial art, thought to be among the oldest in the world, all low stances, high leaps, and combat with staff, sword and shield, performed in a sunken earthen arena. Fast, athletic and thrilling to watch up close; several Fort Kochi venues stage an evening show alongside Kathakali.

items.name: The Kerala Folklore Museum
items.description: A private labour of love built by an antique dealer, its three floors reconstructed in Malabar, Kochi and Travancore styles from salvaged old buildings, holding thousands of masks, sculptures, jewellery, ritual objects and terracotta. The top-floor theatre, under an 18th-century carved wooden ceiling, is one of the most beautiful rooms in the city.

items.name: The Hill Palace Museum
items.description: The former seat of the Cochin royal family, a cluster of buildings across a wooded hilltop, now Kerala's largest archaeological museum, with the royal crowns, jewellery, palanquins, weapons, coins and a family tree of the maharajas. Deer park and gardens make it an easy, uncrowded half-day slightly out of town.

items.name: Marine Drive promenade
items.description: The mainland's breezy waterfront walkway facing the harbour and the islands, with the Rainbow and Chinese-net-shaped footbridges, ferry jetties and evening food carts. The go-to spot for sunset on the Ernakulam side and to catch a public ferry across to Fort Kochi or Vypin, cheap, breezy and local.

items.name: A Kochi harbour & backwater sunset cruise
items.description: A late-afternoon boat out across the harbour mouth, past Willingdon and Bolgatty islands, the naval ships and the fishing-net line, timed for the sun going down over the Arabian Sea. Public ferries do it for a few rupees; a chartered or houseboat sundowner does it in privacy with a drink in hand.

items.name: The Ernakulathappan (Ernakulam Shiva) Temple
items.description: The city temple that gives Ernakulam its name, on Durbar Hall Road near the waterfront, its Shiva idol held to be swayambhu (self-manifested). A working temple at the centre of town, especially alive during the eight-day Utsavam festival with its caparisoned elephants. (Traditional dress; non-Hindus should check entry etiquette.)

items.name: David Hall gallery & cafe
items.description: A restored 17th-century Dutch bungalow on the Parade Ground, run as a contemporary art gallery with a leafy garden cafe, one of the anchors of Kochi's living art scene and a recurring Biennale venue. A civilised place to pause over coffee between exhibitions.

items.name: Kashi Art Cafe & Gallery
items.description: The artsy heart of Fort Kochi since the 1990s, a Dutch-era house that is equal parts gallery and much-loved cafe, a hub for the town's painters, curators and the Biennale crowd. Come for the rotating shows and stay for the courtyard breakfast.

items.name: The Kochi-Muziris Biennale (seasonal)
items.description: India's largest contemporary-art event, held every couple of years across the old spice warehouses of Fort Kochi, Mattancherry and Willingdon Island, Aspinwall House, Pepper House, Anand Warehouse and more. The sixth edition, 'For The Time Being', runs December 2025 to March 2026; if your dates align it transforms the whole town into a walkable exhibition.

items.name: Aspinwall House
items.description: A sprawling waterfront former trading-company estate, coir godowns, a bungalow and a jetty right on the harbour, and the flagship venue of the Biennale. Even between editions the scale and the sea-facing grounds are worth the walk; in season it holds the headline installations.

items.name: Bolgatty Palace & island
items.description: A 1744 Dutch garden mansion on its own island in the harbour, reckoned among the oldest surviving Dutch palaces outside the Netherlands, now a KTDC heritage hotel with a small golf course, pool and lawns running to the water. A short ferry hop for a lunch or a drink with a straight view back to the city skyline.

items.name: Willingdon Island
items.description: A British-era man-made island built from harbour dredgings, named for a viceroy, and still home to the port, the Southern Naval Command and grand old dame hotels. More a texture of Kochi than a ticked sight, but the waterside setting and the Taj Malabar's harbour-facing terrace make a fine, quiet sundowner.

items.name: Vypin Island
items.description: One of the string of islands that make up Kochi, reached by a two-minute ferry from Fort Kochi and worth it for the drive out to Cherai, the old Portuguese Pallipuram Fort and the sea-and-backwater strip. Rural, breezy and a world away from the town in minutes.

items.name: Cherai Beach
items.description: A long, calm golden strand on the northern tip of Vypin where the Arabian Sea and the backwaters run almost side by side, palm-fringed, good for a swim, with dolphins sometimes offshore. About an hour from the centre; the least touristed easy beach day from Kochi and lovely at sundown.

items.name: Pallipuram Fort
credentials: Oldest surviving European fort in India (built 1503)
items.description: The oldest surviving European fort in India, a small hexagonal Portuguese watchtower from 1503 on the northern tip of Vypin. It is a modest, off-the-map stop, but for anyone tracing the coast's colonial history it is the literal starting point, and it pairs naturally with Cherai just down the road.

items.name: Mangalavanam Bird Sanctuary
items.description: A pocket of protected mangrove wetland tucked improbably behind the High Court in the middle of the city, the 'green lung of Kochi', with a walking trail and a watchtower for egrets, herons, cormorants and migratory waders. A surprising, cool, ten-minute escape from downtown for anyone who likes birds.

items.name: An Ayurveda treatment
items.description: Kerala is the home of Ayurveda, and Kochi is where most trips begin it, from a single restorative abhyanga oil massage or shirodhara at a Fort Kochi spa to a multi-day panchakarma programme at a dedicated centre. A natural, unforced way to slow the pace, especially at the start or end of a wider Kerala loop.

items.name: A spice-garden & plantation experience
items.description: Hands-on visits to working spice gardens and cooking sessions let you follow pepper, cardamom, cinnamon and vanilla from vine to kitchen, then cook a Kerala meal, the coastal vegetarian and seafood layers, from appam and stew to the Syrian-Christian and Mappila kitchens. A rich, tactile afternoon and easy to arrange for a family.

items.name: Fort Kochi's colonial cemeteries & Dutch Cemetery
items.description: The walled Dutch Cemetery near the beach, consecrated in 1724, among the oldest European cemeteries in India, with weathered tombs of the traders and soldiers who died far from home. A quiet, atmospheric ten minutes for anyone drawn to the human side of the town's layered history.

items.name: Munnar & the tea estates (day trip / overnight)
credentials: Western Ghats, UNESCO World Heritage Site (natural)
items.description: About four hours up into the hills, a sea of manicured tea gardens rolling over the ridges, with the old Tata tea museum, misty viewpoints and cool mountain air, a complete change of register from the coast. The high ranges here sit within the Western Ghats, and it rewards an overnight far more than a rushed day.

items.name: An Alleppey backwater houseboat
items.description: The classic Kerala experience, a converted kettuvallam rice barge drifting the palm-lined canals and lagoons of Vembanad, meals cooked aboard, the day slipping by from the deck. About 90 minutes south of Kochi; a private overnight houseboat is one of the most peaceful, self-contained luxuries in India, ideal for couples or a family who want the water to themselves.

items.name: Kumarakom backwaters & bird sanctuary
items.description: The quieter, more polished side of Lake Vembanad, a cluster of luxury backwater resorts and a small ornithological sanctuary on former estate land, with egrets, herons, darters and winter migrants. Calmer and greener than Alleppey; a fine base for a slow lakeside couple of days and a village canoe ride.

items.name: Athirappilly Falls (day trip)
items.description: Kerala's largest waterfall, a broad curtain plunging some 80 feet through rainforest, often called the 'Niagara of India' and a much-filmed backdrop. About two hours from Kochi, thunderous just after the monsoon; combine it with the smaller Vazhachal falls and the forest drive for a full day out.

items.name: Thattekad Bird Sanctuary (day trip)
items.description: Salim Ali's favourite birding ground, a lowland-forest sanctuary on the Periyar with an exceptional density of species, Malabar endemics, hornbills, owls and kingfishers among hundreds recorded. Around two hours out; a dawn walk with a local guide is the way to do it, a serious draw for keen birders.

items.name: The Muziris Heritage Trail
items.description: A cluster of sites around the lost 2,000-year-old Roman-trade port of Muziris, the Pattanam excavations, the Paravur synagogue and Jew Street, Kottappuram and Pallipuram forts, old churches and mosques, several turned into small museums. For the historically curious it is the deep back-story of the whole Malabar spice coast, an easy self-driven day north of the city.

items.name: Guruvayur Sri Krishna Temple (day trip)
items.description: One of the most revered Krishna temples in India, about 90 minutes to two hours north, a major Vaishnavite pilgrimage centre famous for its temple elephants and its steady flow of devotees. A meaningful stop for the observant; note it is open to Hindus only, with a traditional dress code.

items.name: Thrissur & the Vadakkunnathan Temple (day trip)
items.description: Kerala's cultural capital, about 75 km north, built around the ancient hilltop Vadakkunnathan Shiva temple, a superb example of Kerala's tiered wooden temple architecture, and home to the spectacular Thrissur Pooram elephant festival each spring. The temple interior is open to Hindus only, but the mound, the grounds and the town's museums reward the trip.

items.name: Chottanikkara Bhagavathy Temple (day trip)
items.description: A famous Devi temple about 20 km from the city where the goddess is worshipped in three forms across the day, Saraswati at dawn, Lakshmi at noon, Durga at dusk, drawing pilgrims from across the south. An atmospheric, deeply local temple visit close enough to fold into a half-day. (Traditional dress; open to Hindus.)

items.name: Broadway Market
items.description: Ernakulam's dense old bazaar street, spices, textiles, gold, provisions and Kerala snacks sold cheek by jowl, the mainland counterpoint to Fort Kochi's polish. A vivid, unvarnished slice of everyday Kochi commerce and the best place to pick up graded spices and coir on the city side.

items.name: A Kerala cooking & appam breakfast experience
items.description: Kochi is the gateway to Kerala's food, lace-edged appam with vegetable stew, Syrian-Christian and Mappila dishes, Fort Kochi's fish grilled fresh from the nets, and one of India's most vegetarian-friendly coastlines besides. A home-kitchen class or a guided food walk turns a meal into the trip's most memorable afternoon.

items.name: A country-boat village backwater trip
items.description: For the backwaters without the drive south, small dugout canoes thread the narrow canals and coir-making villages just outside the city, quieter and more intimate than a big houseboat, gliding under low palms past paddy and toddy shops. A gentle half-day, especially good with children or grandparents.

items.name: Cochin Club & the Fort Kochi green
items.description: The old British-era Cochin Club and the wide parade-ground green behind the seafront, cricket on the grass, rain trees, and the genteel bones of colonial club life still intact. Not a ticketed sight but the calmest corner of Fort Kochi for a stroll and a sense of how the town once lived.

items.name: The Malabar Junction
credentials: Relais & Châteaux restaurant, at The Malabar House
Carnatic / Hindustani music or classical dance at dinner (cooler months)
items.description: Fort Kochi's Relais & Châteaux table, Keralan produce and Mediterranean technique, served to courtyard music.

items.name: Rice Boat
credentials: Taj Malabar Resort & Spa, its signature restaurant
Long-renowned for Kerala coastal and seafood cooking
items.description: The Taj's celebrated Kerala seafood room, shaped like a traditional rice barge over the harbour water.

items.name: History
credentials: Signature restaurant at Brunton Boatyard (CGH Earth)
Menu built from the recipes of Fort Kochi's 32 historic communities
items.description: CGH Earth's storytelling kitchen, dishes drawn from the 32 communities who made Fort Kochi, from Syrian Christian to Jewish to Dutch.

items.name: Kashi Art Café
credentials: Established 1997, a pioneering Kochi art-café institution
Kochi-Muziris Biennale patron, with a working front gallery
items.description: The café that launched Fort Kochi's art scene in 1997, coffee, cake and a gallery, a Biennale patron since the start.

items.name: Fort House Restaurant
credentials: Waterfront pier-side restaurant on the Fort Kochi harbour
Renowned for charcoal-grilled Kerala seafood
items.description: An open-air deck on the harbour pier, charcoal-grilled seafood with big ships passing on their way to sea.

items.name: Dal Roti
credentials: Featured in Lonely Planet
A long-standing Fort Kochi institution on Lily Street
items.description: A beloved heritage-house institution for North Indian rolls and thalis, Lonely Planet's Fort Kochi favourite.

items.name: Qissa Café
credentials: A well-regarded Fort Kochi café
Artist-run in spirit, paintings on the walls, an unhurried room
items.description: A quiet, art-hung café in the fort, good coffee, breakfast and sandwiches, named for the Persian word for 'story'.

items.name: The bar at Brunton Boatyard
credentials: Inside Brunton Boatyard (CGH Earth), on the Fort Kochi harbourfront
Heritage-hotel setting overlooking the water and the fishing nets
items.description: A composed harbour-side drink at CGH Earth's heritage flagship, the most atmospheric evening in Fort Kochi.

items.name: Mattancherry Bar, Taj Malabar
credentials: Inside Taj Malabar Resort & Spa, Cochin
Taj bar service, waterfront setting
items.description: The city's most polished cocktail room, Taj standards and harbour views on Willingdon Island.

items.name: Fort Kochi rooftop cafés
credentials: Rooftop cafés across the Fort Kochi heritage quarter
The definitive Fort Kochi evening, sunset over the harbour and Chinese fishing nets
items.description: Not bars but the fort's real evening, coffee or a sundowner on a heritage rooftop as the light goes over the harbour and the nets.

plan.heading: 3 days in Kochi, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Check into Brunton Boatyard on the harbour, then walk the Chinese fishing nets and St Francis Church before the day heats up.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Mattancherry Palace murals and the Paradesi Synagogue on Jew Town's Synagogue Lane, ending among the antique dealers.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A Kathakali performance at the Kerala Kathakali Centre, arriving early for the make-up, then dinner of Kerala prawns at the Rice Boat.

days.label: Day 2
days.title: Spice history and the backwater edge

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The spice warehouses and pepper exchange of Mattancherry with a trader who knows the trade's history, then coffee at a colonial-era godown.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A private country-boat afternoon through the quieter Kumbalangi canals, seeing the coir-making and Chinese nets away from the crowds.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Sundowners on the Brunton Boatyard verandah over the harbour, then a seafood dinner cooked to your catch.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The galleries and installations of the Kochi-Muziris Biennale trail around Aspinwall House and Pepper House, unhurried.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Cross to Ernakulam for a tailored Kerala Sadhya lunch, then the boutiques and coffee of the newer town.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A quiet last dinner at Malabar Junction in the Malabar House courtyard.

items.name: Fort Kochi
items.description: The atmospheric heritage peninsula of boutique stays and cafes; best for walking and art.

items.name: Mattancherry
items.description: The spice-trade and antiques quarter next door; suits those who want texture and history.

items.name: Marine Drive / Ernakulam
items.description: The modern city across the water; for shopping, dining and transport links rather than heritage.

events.name: Cochin Carnival
events.note: A ten-day Fort Kochi street festival ending on New Year's Eve with the burning of the Pappanji effigy.

events.name: Kochi-Muziris Biennale
events.note: India's leading contemporary-art event, staged in warehouses and heritage buildings across the fort.

events.name: Onam
events.note: Kerala's grand harvest festival, with flower carpets, feasts and boat races across the region.

events.name: Thrissur Pooram (nearby)
events.note: The spectacular caparisoned-elephant temple festival is a short trip north, among India's grandest.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Base yourself in a Fort Kochi heritage house rather than the commercial Ernakulam side; light linen and closed shoes suit the humidity, and the Chinese fishing nets are best at first light or sunset.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Cochin International Airport (COK), about an hour's chauffeured drive to Fort Kochi; the airport is solar-run and unhurried.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with driver for the mainland, and country-boat or ferry crossings between the islands and Fort Kochi, where walking suits the Dutch and Portuguese quarters.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Reliable Jio and Airtel 4G/5G throughout; a local SIM from the airport covers you across Kerala.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Indian rupee; cards are widely accepted in Fort Kochi and Ernakulam, with cash useful for spice markets and ferries; tipping is light.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: November to February is the kind season, dry with 17-30C days; avoid June-September, when the southwest monsoon hits this windward coast hard, and the humid March-May heat.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Cochin International (COK) is well-connected: direct from Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru (about 3, 2 and 1.5 hrs), plus Gulf hubs. IndiGo, Air India and Akasa fly it; for business/first, route via a Gulf carrier (Emirates through Dubai) or use a flagship lounge at your metro origin, as COK's lounges are modest.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No special vaccinations beyond routine Hepatitis A/Typhoid; mosquito cover is sensible in the wet months. Safe, easy port city. Drink sealed or filtered water and be mindful of humidity.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Very easy for vegetarians, with Kerala sadya (banana-leaf thali) and abundant South Indian food; Jain is understood in the better hotels and restaurants. Kashi Art Cafe and the veg sadya at Fort Kochi's heritage tables are genuinely good.
